lessons.title: Math is Mine
lessons.objective: I can describe the ways we are all doers of math, and compare my math story with a classmate's.
lessons.languageObjective: I can tell my math story using the words strength, challenge, and I use math when ___ .

concept.heading: We are all doers of math
concept.intro: Before any new mathematics, the book asks a different question: where does math already live in your day?
concept.keyIdea: Math Practices: Mindset & Problem Solving. 1. Make sense of the problem and persevere in solving it. 2. Look for entry points and decompose complex tasks into manageable parts. 3. Use estimation and mental math to check for reasonableness

worked.title: Watch me estimate the Ferris wheel
lines: The Ferris wheel has 20 cars, and about 4 people fit in each car. About how many people can ride at one time?
I count the cars: 20. Then I estimate how many riders fit in one car: about 4.
I do not count every person — an estimate is a reasoned answer that is close enough to be useful.
linesEs: La rueda de la fortuna tiene 20 cabinas y en cada una caben unas 4 personas. ¿Aproximadamente cuántas personas pueden subir a la vez?
Cuento las cabinas: 20. Luego estimo cuántas personas caben en una cabina: unas 4.
No cuento a cada persona — una estimación es una respuesta razonada que se acerca lo suficiente para ser útil.
worked.titleEs: Mírame estimar la rueda de la fortuna

together.title: Let's decompose 78.5 together
lines: Every one of those is the same number wearing different clothes. Find two more.
linesEs: Cada una de esas es el mismo número con ropa distinta. Halla dos más.

vocabulary.definition: Anyone who uses mathematical thinking — which is everyone, every day.
vocabulary.example: Splitting a bill 4 ways at dinner — that is a doer of math.

vocabulary.definition: Your own history with mathematics — what you have done, felt, and learned so far.
vocabulary.example: “In 3rd grade I hated fractions; this year I can explain them.”

vocabulary.definition: Something you already do well and can share with others.
vocabulary.example: “I am good at mental math with money” — a strength you can teach.

vocabulary.definition: To break a number into parts that add, subtract, multiply, or divide back to it.
vocabulary.example: 78.5 = 70 + 8.5, and also 157 ÷ 2 — both rebuild the same number.

vocabulary.definition: A reasoned answer that is close enough to be useful, without counting every one.
vocabulary.example: 20 cars × about 4 riders ≈ 80 people on the Ferris wheel.

lessons.title: Math is Exploring and Thinking
lessons.objective: I can make sense of a problem, plan a strategy, and use fractions of a whole number to compare quantities.
lessons.languageObjective: I can explain my plan using the words we know, we don't know, and my strategy is ___ .

concept.heading: Make sense, plan, check
concept.intro: The book opens with two warm-ups: about how many peas are in the picture, and decompose 105.76 five different ways. Both are about thinking before computing.
concept.keyIdea: Math Practices: Sense Making & Strategy Planning. 1. Identify known quantities and the unknown question. 2. Choose a strategy (draw a model, write an equation, or build a table). 3. Evaluate progress and pivot to an alternate approach if needed

worked.title: Watch me estimate the peas
lines: A bowl is full of peas — far too many to count one at a time. About how many peas are in the bowl?
I do not count every pea — I look for a group I CAN count, like one small cluster of about 10.
Then I ask how many of those clusters would cover the whole bowl. I count about 12.
12 clusters of about 10 is 12 × 10 = 120, so my estimate is about 120 peas — a reasoned answer, close enough to be useful.
linesEs: Un tazón está lleno de chícharos — demasiados para contarlos uno por uno. ¿Aproximadamente cuántos chícharos hay en el tazón?
No cuento cada chícharo — busco un grupo que sí pueda contar, como un montoncito de unos 10.
Luego me pregunto cuántos de esos montoncitos cubrirían todo el tazón. Cuento unos 12.
12 montoncitos de unos 10 son 12 × 10 = 120, así que mi estimación es de unos 120 chícharos — una respuesta razonada, lo bastante cercana para ser útil.

together.title: Let's decompose 105.76 five ways
lines: Same number, five different breaks. Find one more of your own.
linesEs: El mismo número, cinco descomposiciones distintas. Halla una más por tu cuenta.

vocabulary.definition: An amount in a problem — a number with a meaning attached, like 540 meters.
vocabulary.example: 540 meters — the number 540 AND what it measures.

vocabulary.definition: How two quantities compare or connect to each other.
vocabulary.example: 1 hour → 48 km, 2 hours → 96 km: as one grows, so does the other.

vocabulary.definition: A plan for how to solve a problem before you start computing.
vocabulary.example: “I will draw a tape diagram first, then divide” — chosen before computing.

vocabulary.definition: A solution that makes sense in the context of the problem.
vocabulary.example: 5/6 of 540 must be under 540, so 450 is reasonable and 650 is not.

vocabulary.definition: To keep working on a problem, checking your progress and adjusting your plan when you get stuck.
vocabulary.example: Stuck on the tram problem → try a tape diagram instead → keep going.

title: The Everyday Math Detective Agency
mission: Find the mathematics hiding in everyday decisions. Build an estimate, test a strategy, and explain why another person could reason differently.
investigate: Before counting, estimate how many seats the seating plan holds. What did you use as an anchor?
Change the rows but keep the total number of seats. Find two different arrangements.
Which arrangement is easier to count? Explain how grouping helps you check your estimate.
create: Design seating for 48 people. Draw two arrangements, explain how you know each fits 48, and describe one math strength you used.

support.prompt: About how many people can ride the Ferris wheel at one time if it has 20 cars that each hold about 4 people?
support.explanation: 20 cars with about 4 riders each is 20 × 4, which is about 80 people.
feedback: That divides 20 by 4 instead of multiplying.
That adds 20 + 4 instead of multiplying.
That multiplies as if each car held 20 people.
hints: How many groups are there, and how big is each group?
20 groups of 4.
Multiply 20 × 4.

support.prompt: Which of these is a correct way to decompose 78.5?
support.explanation: 70 + 8.5 = 78.5. Decomposing means the parts must add back to the original number.
hints: Add each option and see what you get.
The parts must total 78.5 exactly.
Add the two parts in each choice. Which total lands exactly on 78.5?

support.explanation: 80 − 1.5 = 78.5. Decomposing can use subtraction, not only addition.
feedback: 80 + 1.5 = 81.5 — that moves the wrong direction.
hints: Start at 80. How far down is 78.5?
Check your subtraction against each choice: which one starts above 78.5 and takes away exactly that gap?

support.prompt: What does it mean to ESTIMATE how many people are on the Ferris wheel?
choices: Give a reasoned answer that is close enough to be useful
Refuse to answer without more data
support.explanation: An estimate is reasoned, not random, and it does not require counting every one.
feedback: Counting every person exactly is not estimating — that is an exact count.
A random guess uses no reasoning, so it is not an estimate.
Estimating is what you do precisely when you cannot count them all.
hints: Is an estimate exact?
Is an estimate random?
It sits between those two.

support.prompt: Name one way you used math outside of school this week.
support.explanation: I used math when I figured out I needed to leave by 7:40 to catch the bus at 7:55.

support.prompt: Which of these is a correct way to decompose 105.76?
support.explanation: 100 + 5.76 = 105.76. Decomposing means the parts must rebuild the original number exactly.
feedback: 10 + 5.76 = 15.76 — that drops the hundreds digit of 105.76.
100 + 5.076 = 105.076 — that pushes the digits one decimal place too far right.
105 + 7.6 = 112.6, not 105.76 — the 7 and 6 belong in the tenths and hundredths places.
hints: Add each option and compare to 105.76.
The parts must total 105.76 exactly.
Add the two parts in each choice. Only one total lands exactly on 105.76.

support.prompt: Which is another correct decomposition of 105.76?
support.explanation: 110 − 4.24 = 105.76. A decomposition can use subtraction, not only addition.
feedback: 106 − 0.34 = 105.66 — the difference from 106 is 0.24, not 0.34.
110 − 5.24 = 104.76 — that takes away one whole too many.
110 + 4.24 = 114.24 — that moves away from 105.76 instead of down to it.
hints: Start at 110. How far down is 105.76?
So subtracting 4.24 from 110 works.

support.prompt: Deon walked a shorter distance than Miguel, and Evelyn walked a longer distance than Miguel. Who walked the shortest distance?
support.explanation: Deon is below Miguel and Evelyn is above Miguel, so the order is Deon < Miguel < Evelyn — Deon walked the shortest distance.
feedback: Miguel sits in the middle of the three distances, not at either end.
Evelyn walked a LONGER distance than Miguel, so she walked the most, not the least.
It can be determined — the two relationships put all three students in order even without exact numbers.
hints: Put Miguel in the middle and place the other two around him.
Deon is below Miguel; Evelyn is above Miguel.
Who ends up lowest?

support.prompt: The London building will be 5/6 as tall as One World Trade Center, which is 540 meters. How tall will the London building be?
support.explanation: 5/6 × 540: one sixth of 540 is 90, and 5 sixths is 5 × 90 = 450 meters.
feedback: 90 meters is only 1/6 of 540 — you still need to multiply by the 5 in the numerator.
534 meters subtracts 6 from 540 instead of finding 5/6 OF 540.
648 meters is 6/5 of 540 — that flips the fraction and makes the building taller than 540.
hints: First find one sixth of 540.
Now take 5 of those sixths.

support.prompt: In the Comparing Walks problem, name one thing you KNOW and one thing you DON'T know.
support.explanation: I know that Deon walked a shorter distance than Miguel. I don't know how far each student actually walked.

support.prompt: Predict the total spaces for these settings. Give the answer in spaces. Round to four decimal places if needed.
parameters: Seats or tiles in each row: 6
support.explanation: 8 × 6 = 48. Perimeter: 28 units. Count equal rows to find the total.
hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.
Use the relationship you explored in Investigate. Check with a second method.

support.prompt: A ride has 16 cars with 4 seats in each. How many riders fit if every seat is filled?
support.explanation: Sixteen equal groups of four give 16 × 4 = 64. A quick estimate, 15 × 4 = 60, supports the result.
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

support.prompt: You need 48 seats arranged in rows of 6. How many rows do you need?
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

core.prompt: Which decomposition of 78.5 uses multiplication correctly?
core.explanation: 39.25 × 2 = 78.5, so halving and doubling is another way to break the number apart.
feedback: 39 × 2 = 78, which is close but not 78.5.
78.5 × 2 = 157, which doubles the number instead of rebuilding it.
hints: What is half of 78.5?
Half of 78.5 is 39.25.
Two of those halves rebuild it.

core.prompt: A Ferris wheel holds about 78 riders per turn and makes 6 turns an hour. About how many riders per hour?
core.explanation: 78 riders on each of 6 turns is 78 × 6 = 468 riders in an hour.
feedback: That divides 78 by 6 instead of multiplying.
That adds 78 + 6 instead of multiplying.
That multiplies by 10 instead of 6.
hints: Each turn carries a full load. How many turns?
6 turns of 78 riders.

core.prompt: Which statement matches this lesson's big idea?
choices: Only people who are fast at math are doers of math
Math only counts when it happens in a classroom
Everyone is a doer of math, and we do it in different ways
There is one right way to think about a math problem
core.explanation: The lesson's whole point is that everyone already does math, differently, and sharing those differences helps everyone.
feedback: Speed is not what makes someone a doer of math.
The Ferris wheel, the recipe and the bus are all outside a classroom.
Different approaches are exactly what makes sharing worthwhile.
hints: What did the sorting activity show?
Every card belonged in 'this is doing math'.
And people sorted their reasons differently.

core.prompt: You estimate 80 riders and the true count is 78. Was your estimate useful?
choices: No — an estimate is only useful if it is exact
Yes — it was close enough to plan with
Yes — because any answer is fine
core.explanation: 80 and 78 are close enough for planning, which is exactly what an estimate is for.
feedback: Exactness is what a count is for, not an estimate.
Estimating is a real mathematical tool, used constantly.
A good estimate needs reasoning behind it, not just any guess.
hints: How far off were you?
Off by 2 out of about 80.
Close enough to be useful.

core.prompt: Describe three different situations where you use math in your life. Say how the math is the SAME in each one.
core.frame: I use math when I ___ , when I ___ , and when I ___ .
core.explanation: I use math when I cook, when I skate, and when I save money. In all three I am comparing amounts to decide whether I have enough.

core.prompt: The Rio de Janeiro building will be 9/10 as tall as One World Trade Center (540 meters). How tall will it be?
core.explanation: 9/10 × 540: one tenth of 540 is 54, and 9 tenths is 9 × 54 = 486 meters.
feedback: 54 meters is only 1/10 of 540 — you still need 9 of those tenths.
594 meters ADDS one tenth (540 + 54) instead of taking 9 tenths of 540.
4,860 meters multiplies 540 by 9 but never divides by 10.
hints: First find one tenth of 540.
Multiply that tenth by 9.

core.prompt: The Tokyo building will be 6/5 as tall as One World Trade Center (540 meters). How tall will it be?
core.explanation: 6/5 × 540: one fifth of 540 is 108, and 6 fifths is 6 × 108 = 648 meters — taller than 540, because 6/5 is greater than 1.
feedback: 108 meters is only 1/5 of 540 — you still need 6 of those fifths.
432 meters SUBTRACTS a fifth (540 − 108) instead of taking 6 fifths.
450 meters is 5/6 of 540 — that flips the fraction, and it belongs to the London building.
hints: First find one fifth of 540.
6/5 means six of those fifths — will that be more or less than 540?

core.prompt: Without calculating, which new building must be TALLER than One World Trade Center, and why?
choices: London, because 5/6 has a 6 in it
Rio de Janeiro, because 9/10 is close to 1
None — a fraction of 540 is always less than 540
core.explanation: Multiplying 540 by a fraction greater than 1 gives more than 540. Only 6/5 is greater than 1; 5/6 and 9/10 are both less than 1.
feedback: The 6 in 5/6 is the denominator — 5/6 is less than 1, so the London building is SHORTER than 540 meters.
Close to 1 is not greater than 1 — 9/10 of 540 is still less than 540 meters.
A fraction GREATER than 1, like 6/5, makes the product greater than 540.
hints: Compare each fraction to 1.
Multiplying by a fraction greater than 1 makes the result bigger.

core.prompt: You calculate 5/6 × 540 and get 650 meters. What does the checking step of your plan tell you?
choices: The answer is fine because it is close to 540
The answer is fine because 650 is a bigger number than 5/6
The answer is unreasonable — 5/6 of 540 must be LESS than 540
Checking is only needed when the problem asks for it
core.explanation: 5/6 is less than 1, so 5/6 of 540 must land below 540. Getting 650 means the plan needs adjusting — which is exactly what checking is for.
feedback: Close to 540 is not the test — the answer must be BELOW 540, because 5/6 is less than 1.
Comparing 650 to the fraction 5/6 mixes up two different kinds of quantities — compare the answer to 540 instead.
This lesson says we check our progress on EVERY problem, not only when asked.
hints: Is 5/6 more or less than 1?
Multiplying by a fraction less than 1 makes the result smaller.
So should the answer be above or below 540?

core.prompt: Miguel walked 2 miles. Deon walked less than Miguel, and Evelyn walked more than Miguel. Choose possible distances for Deon and Evelyn and explain how you checked both relationships.
core.explanation: Deon walked a shorter distance than Miguel, so Deon could have walked 1.5 miles. Evelyn walked a longer distance than Miguel, so Evelyn could have walked 2.5 miles. I checked: 1.5 < 2 and 2.5 > 2, so both relationships are true.

core.prompt: Predict the total spaces for these settings. Give the answer in spaces. Round to four decimal places if needed.
parameters: Seats or tiles in each row: 6
core.explanation: 9 × 6 = 54. Perimeter: 30 units. Count equal rows to find the total.
hints: Identify which quantities the requested measure uses.

core.explanation: Sixteen equal groups of four give 16 × 4 = 64. A quick estimate, 15 × 4 = 60, supports the result.

core.prompt: You need 48 seats arranged in rows of 6. How many rows do you need?
hints: Name the given quantities and the quantity you need.
Draw a model or write the relationship first. Check your answer in the original situation.

stretch.prompt: Which set shows FIVE different correct decompositions of 78.5?
stretch.explanation: All five in the first set rebuild 78.5 exactly: by addition, by subtraction, by multiplication, and by division.
feedback: 78 + 5 = 83, so that set contains an error.
80 + 1.5 = 81.5, so that set contains an error.
39.25 × 3 = 117.75, so that set contains an error.
hints: Check each member of each set.
One wrong member spoils the whole set.
Find the set where all five land on 78.5.

stretch.prompt: Why does the book start the year with this lesson instead of with computation?
choices: Because there is no mathematics in Unit 1
Because what you believe about yourself shapes how you learn all year
Because sixth graders have forgotten all their math
Because estimating is the hardest skill in the book
stretch.explanation: The lesson's summary says it directly: what we believe about ourselves, about others, and about what we are learning shapes us.
feedback: There is real mathematics here — estimating and decomposing 78.5.
The lesson assumes you bring strengths, not gaps.
Estimating is a tool used all year, not the hardest skill.
hints: Read the Summarize statement again.
It is about belief, not about computation.
Belief shapes the whole year.

stretch.prompt: Someone says “I'm just not a math person.” Using this lesson, write what you would say back.
stretch.explanation: I would say that they already do math every day — deciding if they have enough money, splitting food fairly, judging how long something takes. Being a doer of math is not about speed; it is about that thinking, and they are already doing it.

stretch.prompt: Which set shows FIVE different correct decompositions of 105.76?
stretch.explanation: All five in the first set rebuild 105.76 exactly — by addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division.
feedback: 105 + 7.6 = 112.6, so that set contains an error.
52.88 × 3 = 158.64, so that set contains an error.
hints: Check every member of each set.
One wrong member spoils the whole set.
Find the set where all five land exactly on 105.76.

stretch.prompt: Without computing the exact heights, order the three new buildings from shortest to tallest. (London: 5/6 of 540 m, Rio de Janeiro: 9/10 of 540 m, Tokyo: 6/5 of 540 m.)
stretch.explanation: Compare the fractions: 5/6 ≈ 0.83 is less than 9/10 = 0.9, and both are less than 6/5 = 1.2. Same whole, so the order of the fractions is the order of the heights.
feedback: That puts 9/10 below 5/6 — but 9/10 = 0.9 is GREATER than 5/6 ≈ 0.83.
That is tallest to shortest — the question asks for shortest to tallest.
Tokyo's 6/5 is greater than 1, so Tokyo must be last, not in the middle.
hints: All three are fractions of the SAME 540 meters, so just compare the fractions.
Compare each fraction to 1, then compare 5/6 and 9/10 to each other.

stretch.prompt: A classmate says, "In math, only the final answer matters." Using this lesson, write what you would say back.
stretch.explanation: I would say the thinking matters just as much. In the buildings problem we knew London and Rio would be under 540 meters and Tokyo would be over BEFORE calculating, because we compared the fractions to 1. That checking is what catches mistakes — when we do math, we make sense of problems, check our progress, and try other strategies at dead ends.
